editor_note: Today’s edition asks what keeps an agent or interface trustworthy after the first impressive result. The answers are boundaries, reviewed procedures, honest hardware limits, visible interaction states, and tests that leave room for failure.

stories.title: Agent speed is not the same as a trustworthy workflow
stories.summary: Stack Overflow’s essay says developer tools become trusted when their workflows stay predictable. Agentic tools can produce more, faster, but they are harder to inspect; linters, tests, CI, and team habits still carry the older process, so checking generated code may erase some of the speed gain.
stories.why_it_matters: Speed is a poor substitute for a visible handoff, a testable result, and a way back when an agent gets it wrong.

stories.title: qm separates agent work by person and room
stories.summary: qm is a TypeScript harness for startups that gives each person and room its own scoped memory, files, permissions, crons, web apps, and persistent sandbox. It keeps private and shared work separate while teams collaborate in Slack and on the web, and it can drive multiple agent harnesses instead of locking a deployment to one vendor.
stories.why_it_matters: The separation is the point: shared work can grow without turning every file or memory into a company-wide default.

stories.title: Skill Recorder turns a watched task into reviewed instructions
stories.summary: Microsoft’s Skill Recorder records a work session, uses Copilot CLI to reconstruct the intent and ordered steps, then lets the user review them before it writes a SKILL.md procedure or scheduled Automation. It favors native tools such as gh and web_fetch over replaying clicks, which gives the result a chance to work beyond the original screen.
stories.why_it_matters: Recorded know-how matters more when a person can inspect the procedure before an agent runs it.

stories.title: WASTE runs a 2.78-trillion-parameter model from a 64 GB Mac
stories.summary: WASTE is a dependency-free C engine for mixture-of-experts models. It holds the shared trunk in RAM and streams selected experts from NVMe; its README reports running Kimi K3 on a 64 GB MacBook Pro at about 0.6 tokens per second, with a bounded cache balancing speed and memory.
stories.why_it_matters: The bottleneck shifts from “does it fit?” to storage bandwidth, cache behavior, and a speed trade-off a local machine can expose.

stories.title: Interior makes the wait after a click part of the design
stories.summary: Interior is a copy-in React collection of micro-interactions built on headless hooks with optional styled examples. Its notes reserve space before state changes arrive, match motion to the physical event, treat keyboard input as a full path, handle abandoned gestures, and preserve information when reduced motion is on.
stories.why_it_matters: Trust grows in the small transitions: people should know what changed, what is pending, and what happens if they stop halfway.

stories.title: Talivia ties product behavior to revenue data
stories.summary: Talivia’s open-source edition combines web analytics, Session Replay, collaborators, shared analytics, import/export, and revenue connections for Stripe, LemonSqueezy, Polar, Dodo, Yolfi, or manual payments. It is a self-hosted subset of Talivia Cloud, runs on PostgreSQL, and documents backups before upgrades.
stories.why_it_matters: Analytics gets sharper when a visit, a replay, and a payment can be read in the same conversation.

stories.title: Acquisition sites should start with user jobs
stories.summary: Little Language Models says a multi-company redesign should begin with user goals, not product ownership. Teams write goals for one another, group navigation and content around the actions people need, test labels and hierarchy with a small user group, and reuse content horizontally across pages.
stories.why_it_matters: A merger is an information-architecture problem before it is a branding problem: start with what people came to do.

stories.title: Pelican makes spatial reasoning visible
stories.summary: Karpathy’s Pelican post presents a pelican-on-a-bike scene as a test of whether models can build a convincing result through code and spatial reasoning rather than a video-generation pipeline. The task makes the model’s handling of objects and their relationships visible instead of hiding it inside a polished video.
stories.why_it_matters: A small scene you can inspect beats a polished demo when the goal is to see where a model loses track of space.
